Abstract:
It is evident that in spite of some similarities the nature of characteristics of the political and 
economic aims of theempires and national states are different. It seems that in spite of some 
similarities in the aims, political economies and the institutions there are also some very critical 
differences between the Ottoman world and Western capitalist nations.While the Western 
European nations followed the protectionist mercantilist policies the Ottomans followed an open 
door economic policies towards the Atlantic nations in the early modern times.When we look at 
the institutions we have seen the waqfs, cash waqfs, ahidnames (capitulations), brotherhood (ahilik), 
iltizam, malikane and esham systems, etc. in the Ottoman world while the joint stock companies, 
modern banks based on interest, insurance companies and exchange stock market appeared in 
North Atlantic World in in the early modern times. These institutions played different roles in 
between the two worlds and civilisations. Especially the Ottoman cash waqfs are very critical as the 
first modern islamic bank institutions

The History of Islamic Finance Between Two Business Models: 
Sixties vs. Seventies Lessons for the Future
Prof Dr. Ahmed Belouafi
King Abdulaziz University, 
Jeddah, Saudi Arabia
ambelouafi@kau.edu.sa
Abstract:
Through deductive, inductive, and analytical methodologies the paper aims to explore the early 
inception of Islamic financial institutions (IFIs) initiatives in the Modern era in Muslim countries. 
It is well documented in the literature of Islamic banking and finance that the birth of IFIs 
occurred in two stages: in the sixties and the seventies of the 20th century respectively. The sixties 
saw the establishment of two organizations in two countries based on different aims and 
aspirations. However, they share a common feature of the 'local orientation' character in serving 
well-defined objectives for a specific geographical territory. These are: the local saving bank or the 
local development bank at Mit-Ghamr in the Delta Nile province in Egypt and the Tabung Haji 
(Haj fund) in Malaysia. In contrast, the seventies experiment started with the establishment of 
Dubai Islamic Bank in 1975 and, it was based on the universal business model of a typical 
commercial bank that has been working for centuries in the West. Rather than focusing on a 
historical narration of the development of IFIs over time in different locations, the paper took, a 
somewhat, heterodox approach that intends to serve twofold:(1) –carry out a quick comparison 
between the core business models of the two experiments, and (2) – to draw some lessons for the 
future directions for the development of IFIs. 
Keywords: local saving banks, Tabung Haji, Mit-Ghamr, commercial bank, business model, Egypt, 
Malaysia

The Evolution of the Islamic Banking Industry Over Five Decades (1975–2025)
Dr. Abdelkader Chachi
Sabahattin Zaim University
 Istanbul, Turkey
abdelkader.chachi@izu.edu.tr
Abstract:
Objective: This research paper—presented at the 16th Conference of the International Association 
for Islamic Economics, under the theme "The Islamic Financial Industry After Fifty Years of 
Practice", held in the historic city of Sétif (Algeria) from May 13 to 15, 2025—aims to shed light 
on the various stages experienced by Islamic banking services over the past five decades. It covers 
the early revival attempts prior to 1975, then progresses through subsequent stages starting from 
1975—the year Islamic banking began to stabilize, yield results, and gain international 
recognition—up to the year 2025. Additionally, the paper seeks to present and discuss some of the 
challenges Islamic banking has faced since the early 20th century.
Methodology: This paper adopts a combination of complementary scientific methodologies, 
depending on the writing context. It begins with an inductive-deductive approach, involving a 
critical reading and in-depth analysis of the literature on the development of Islamic banking 
services worldwide from 1975 to 2025. It also employs a descriptive-analytical method to describe 
and analyze the stages of development and challenges faced—or still being faced—by Islamic 
banking since the early 20th century in various regions of the world. This is done using SWOT 
analysis (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats) for each stage. Additionally, the 
historical method is used to connect information in a clearly defined chronological sequence.
Findings: Through the presentation, discussion, and analysis of the historical and regional 
development of Islamic banking services worldwide, the study revealed the following:
First, banking operations (such as deposits, loans, debts, transfers, and currency exchange) are not 
recent innovations, as many economists believe. In fact, these operations were well-known and 
practiced by many ancient civilizations, including the Sumerians, Babylonians, Chinese, Egyptians, 
Greeks, Romans, and Muslims.
Second, the first attempt to establish an Islamic bank in the 20th century occurred in Algeria in 
1929, when Muslim scholars from the Association of Muslim Scholars and some Algerian 
businessmen prepared everything necessary to launch it. However, French colonial authorities 
prevented the attempt from materializing.
Third, modern Islamic banking operations, which began in the second half of the 1970s, continue 
to grow and expand rapidly. They are expected to sustain high average annual growth rates in the 
future.
Keywords: Islamic economics, Islamic banking and finance, Islamic finance, banks.

History and Evolution of Islamic Finance Industry in the World
Dr. Sanaullah Ansari
SZABIST University,
Islamabad, Pakistan
sanaullahansari@hotmail.com
Abstract:
Islamic Finance or Islamic Financial System is based upon social welfare. The guiding principles of 
this system have been given in Holy Quran by Almighty Allah and in Hadith by Holy Prophet 
(PBUH). The major difference between Islamic and conventional finance is Riba (Interest) which is 
prohibited in Islam. Islamic finance industry is comprising of Islamic Banking, Islamic Insurance 
(Takaful), Islamic Capital Markets and Islamic Funds. Historically, Riba-free transactions were 
started and encouraged by Holy Prophet (PBUH)himself in 7th Century. Later, in 9th Century, 
Hawala system was practiced in Baghdad which is trust based money transfer system. 
By the passing of time, Islamic finance industry evolved and very first Islamic Bank, Mit Ghamr 
Savings Bank was established in Egypt in 1963 to provide Riba-free products and services. Naseer 
Social Bank was also founded in Egypt in 1971 which was based upon Sharia’h principles. Dubai 
Islamic Bank was established in 1975 which was the beginning of modern Islamic finance industry 
in the world. To provide financial strength to Muslim countries, Islamic Development Bank was 
established in Saudi Arabia in 1977. In the same year, International Association of Islamic Banks 
(IAIB) was established in Saudi Arabia to promote Islamic finance industry. Malaysia jumped into 
this industry by establishing very first Islamic bank, Bank Islam Malaysia Berhad in 1983. 
Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI) was founded in 
1991 in Bahrain to develop Shariah compliant accounting and auditing standards to be practiced 
by Islamic financial institutions throughout the world. Islamic Financial Services Board(IFSB) was 
established in Malaysia in 2002 to develop rules and regulations of this industry. The very first 
Islamic bank in Pakistan, Meezan Bank was established in 2002. Islamic finance industry is now 
established in almost all Muslim countries. Islamic Bank of Britain is the first Islamic retail bank 
which was established in Europe in 2004. Presently, around 150 Islamic financial institutions are 
operating in Europe, including banks, insurance companies, and investment funds in UK, France, 
Germany, Italy, Spain, Norway, Sweden, Luxemburg, and Greece. Similarly, around 43 Islamic 
financial institutions are also working in USA. 
By the end of 2023, Islamic finance industry is expanded to 1,981 financial institutions with total 
assets of $4.925 trillion. This includes Islamic banking with618 banks and $3,569 billion assets, 
Sukuk $863 billion, Islamic Funds $254 billion, Other IFIs $153 billion and Takaful $86 billion 
assets. Iran is the leading contributor in Islamic finance industry by having 42% of the total assets 
of Islamic banking. The growth rate of Islamic finance industry worldwide is 11% which is 
remarkable achievement. The reason of this extra-ordinary growth is the development of profit-
sharing products which are based on partnership modes. Therefore, it is expected that the assets of 
Islamic finance industry will reach $7.528 trillion by 2028 which is the success of this industry 
worldwide.

‏أنموذجا‏
The Role of Supporting Financial Institutions: The Accounting and 
Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI) as a 
Model
Prof Dr. Elyes Dardour
University of Ez-Zitouna, Tunisia 
Abstract:
This scientific paper explores the critical role of supporting financial institutions in strengthening 
the infrastructure of the Islamic finance industry, with a particular focus on the Accounting and 
Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI) as a case study. It outlines the 
emergence and functions of various supporting bodies, ranging from awareness, training, and 
rating to standard-setting in both Shari’ah and accounting. The paper delves into AAOIFI as the 
first international non-profit body established to issue accounting and Shari’ah standards for 
Islamic financial institutions. To date, it has produced over 60 Shari’ah standards, in addition to 
accounting, governance, and ethical standards. The study explains AAOIFI’s organizational 
structure, including the Board of Trustees, the Shari’ah Board, and standards boards, detailing their 
respective mandates. It highlights the scholarly efforts supporting AAOIFI’s work through 
preparatory studies, legal appendices, and curriculum development. Furthermore, the paper 
emphasizes AAOIFI’s role in human capital development through its certified professional 
programs, such as the Certified Shari’ah Auditor and the Certified Islamic Professional Accountant. 
It concludes that AAOIFI has significantly contributed to institutionalizing and standardizing 
Islamic financial practices, thereby enhancing trust among stakeholders and regulators

The Role of AAOIFI Financial Accounting Standards in Harmonizing 
and Standardizing Practices and Promoting Shariah Compliance
Dr. Mohammad Hajj Bakir
Accounting and Auditing Organization for 
Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI)
Manama, Bahrain
Abstract:
AAOIFI Financial accounting standards (FAS) constitute a set of principles-based provisions that 
are general in nature, which prescribe and regulate accounting treatments (recognition, 
measurement, subsequent measurement as well as presentation and disclosures) for Islamic finance 
transactions and all related events and conditions. At times, FAS may prescribe rules-based 
provisions for cases that require specific Shari’ah rulings (ahkam).
Being a level much sophisticated and cherished by a standard-setting like AAOIFI, standardization 
is a multi-faceted process that involves creating the minimum level of generally accepted practices 
as a reference point that market players have to comply with in their financial reporting that 
reflect their unique business model and adherence to the principles and rules of Shari’ah. It is a 
consciously undertaking process that involves a degree of trusteeship by accredited watchdogs.
The benefits of standardization are plentiful, including particularly industry moving in one 
direction towards realisation of Maqasid Al Shari’ah, industry not compromising on the minimum 
level of Shari’ah-compliance in all areas of operations, industry adopting the best practices, 
industry enjoying the trust and confidence of its stakeholders and industry remaining stable, 
sustainable, and competitive.
Accounting is central to Islam because all actions are counted by Allah. Primary accountability is to 
Allah as all of one's actions (good and bad deeds) in life will be accounted for on the Day of 
Judgement. The role of accounting, as a set of conventions and treatment methodologies, is 
essential, as it helps verify that financial transactions adhere to Shariah principles through proper 
recording and disclosure. Shari’ah provides core Shari’ah principles and rules applicable to IF 
transactions, and on accounting side, this is meant to ensure that the products and services are 
executed, recorded and presented in the right manner and reflect the right characteristics. The need 
for Islamic accounting stems from multiple aspects including catering to specific information 
needs, the need to define what is the real true and fair view, transaction trail – and compliance, 
risk profile of the transactions, balances, and profit and loss and balances determination in line 
with Shari’ah, as well as the implications of reputation risk.

Jurisdictional Challenges in the Islamic Financial Industry: Foreign 
Courts vs. Islamic Arbitration 
Rami Suliman Ibrahim Abudaqqa
International Islamic Centre for Reconciliation and 
Arbitration
 (IICRA), UAE
Abstract:
An evaluation of the Islamic finance experience over fifty years in the field of resolving disputes 
arising from Islamic finance, where the researcher employed the inductive, comparative, and 
analytical methods. The study was divided into an introduction, two main sections, a conclusion, 
and a list of sources and references. Among the most important findings of the study is that the 
establishment of an integrated legislative framework contributes to empowering Islamic banking 
transactions and avoids conflicts between Sharia and legal rulings at the international level. The 
growth and prosperity of Islamic finance has led to an increase in disputes, making it urgently 
necessary to qualify specialized personnel capable of resolving such disputes, combining Sharia, 
legal, and financial expertise. In the absence of a comprehensive legislative system regulating 
Islamic finance and the lack of specialized judiciary, arbitration is considered the most suitable 
means for settling Islamic finance disputes. 
The study recommended: completing the issuance of laws and regulations governing Islamic 
finance, preparing qualified personnel, including an Islamic arbitration clause in contracts of 
Islamic financial institutions, and adopting a legal auditing methodology for Islamic financial 
products.

Purpose: The purpose of this Paper is to present, describe, expose, discuss and analyse the role of 
the Islamic Foundation-UK in the development and promotion of Islamic economics, banking and 
finance during the last fifty years (1975-2025) and to shed some light on one of the most 
distinguished Islamic institutions in the West.
Objective: The aim and objective of this paper is to expose and make public some of the 
information that a lot of people do not know or realize about the role and functions of the Islamic 
Foundation-UK since its establishment, and highlight some of its milestones and positive role in 
advancing, promoting and pushing the spread and development of Islamic economics, banking and 
finance, not only in the UK, where it is based, but in many parts of the world. 
Methodology: This paper follows a number of methodologies, depending on the context of the 
writing. It starts with and inductive-deductive methodology, by critically reading and analysing 
what has been written about the Islamic Foundation-UK from different quarters. Secondly, the 
paper also follows the descriptive-analytical methodology to describe and analyse the role of the 
Islamic Foundation-UK in the development and promotion of Islamic economics, banking and 
finance during the last fifty years (1975-2025) and lastly the paper also follows the historical 
methodology to relate the information in a historical sequence.
Findings: From the presentation, discussion and analysis of the operations, functions and role of 
the Islamic Foundation-UK, it is found that, the Islamic Foundation-UK is one of the oldest 
research and training centres to promote Islamic economics, banking and finance since its 
foundation, more than fifty years (1973-2025) and that it published the earliest books written by 
Islamic economics pioneers such as Muhammad Nejatullah Siddiqi, Khurshid Ahmad, Muhammad 
Umer Chapra, Fahim Khan, Munawar Iqbal and others. It, also, organised Orientation Courses, 
Seminars and Conferences on Islamic Economics, Banking and Finance, sponsored the teaching of 
the subject at a highly ranked British University, Loughborough University in 1996 and established 
a specialised Institute in the year 2000, called Markfield Institute of Higher Education that offers 
among other courses, Master and PhD degrees in Islamic Economics, banking and Finance.   
Recommendations: It is very much recommended to get to know the Islamic Foundation-UK even 
more and help it in one way or the other in fulfilling its tasks and in realizing its aims and 
objectives, especially in the promotion of Islamic Economics, Banking and Finance
Keywords: Islamic Foundation-UK, Islamic Economics, Islamic Banking. Islamic Finance.

‏الحوكمة الشرعة في المؤسسات المالية اإلسالمية :الواقع وآفاق المستقبل‏
Sharīah Governance of Islamic Financial Institutions: A Review and 
Evaluation
Dr. El Ayachi Feddad
Abstract:
The final decades of the last century, at both financial and economic levels, were marked by 
pervasive corruption infiltrating the very fabric of institutions and corporations. This corruption 
extended even to oversight and rating agencies, and its cumulative effect led to the emergence of 
financial crises whose severity varied over time. The most severe of these struck the entire world at 
the beginning of the past millennium, and its repercussions continue to this day. Despite 
interventions and economic and financial policies by international financial institutions, they have 
been unable to curb these reverberations—evidenced most clearly by the crippling economic crises 
afflicting some countries, which in certain cases have driven them to the brink of bankruptcy 
without any definitive resolution. Humanity has reaped nothing from these crises but ruin and 
devastation.
The deterioration of institutional and corporate conditions, the absence of values and ideals within 
their systems, and the misconduct of supervisory and executive personnel—combined with new 
forms of corruption aimed at securing illicit gains for owners and shareholders through profit 
maximization by illegal means at times, or by concealing or failing to disclose data that do not 
reflect reality—have all prompted international bodies concerned with monitoring financial and 
economic activity, as well as many individual states, to turn their attention to administrative 
rationalization and corporate governance. These efforts materialized through a series of measures 
and policies that later became known as the Principles of Governance.
Several international economic organizations have taken an interest in establishing governance 
standards. Notably, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) issued 
its “Principles of Corporate Governance” in 1999, followed by an updated version in 2004, which 
has since guided many countries in formulating their institutional regulations, corporate laws, and 
oversight and supervisory standards.
The Islamic financial industry has not remained immune to these standards; indeed, it has 
embraced them with the same rigor as conventional institutions. Islamic financial entities have 
become increasingly diligent in applying governance principles, underpinning them with the 
necessary legislation and regulations. In response, key supporters of the Islamic finance industry—
such as the Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB) in Malaysia, the Accounting and Auditing 
Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI) in Bahrain, and the General Council for 
Islamic Banks and Financial Institutions (CIBAFI) in Bahrain—have swiftly adopted governance 
standards and principles to guide and regulate these financial institutions.

The Role of Governance, Supervisory Boards, and Central Banks in the 
Islamic Finance Industry
Dr. Mohamed Mostafa Ahmed Shoaib

Abstract:
Praise be to Allah and peace and blessings be upon the Messenger of Allah. The industry of Islamic 
finance witnesses rapid development and growth in such a way that it has to be studied in .terms 
of its strength, weakness and how to make it stable. The research has defined the Islamic financial 
industry and its characteristics and components, and governance, Sharia supervisory boards and 
central banks. The research has also shown that each of them has a very important role in the 
development, growth and stability of the Islamic financial industry.  Through governance and 
Sharia supervision controls the actions of officials in Islamic financial institution can be regulated. 
The Central banks function to organise and develop the Islamic financial industry, and their tools 
include: setting regulatory and legislative frameworks and regulations, granting licenses, promoting 
financial and economic inclusion and stability, training, research and development, international 
cooperation, and enhancing confidence in the . Islamic financial industry.
.Keywords: Islamic financial industry, supervisory bodies, central banks, governance

in Light of the Governing Legal Frameworks
Dr. Nacer Soulaimane

dr.nacer25@yahoo.com
Abstract:
This research aims to analyze the subject of digital Islamic banks in terms of their concept, 
requirements for their establishment and importance, as well as the legal texts regulating their

Abstract:
The research provides a significant theoretical and applied contribution to the risk management of 
Islamic crowdfunding platforms, by diagnosing and analyzing the various types of risks facing 
these platforms and the means to manage and mitigate them. It focuses on the case study of the 
Saudi platform "Manafa", one of the most prominent licensed platforms in the field of debt 
crowdfunding, and is classified as compliant with the provisions of Islamic Sharia.

of compliance with Sharia law, given that they operate based on the rules and regulations of 
Islamic financial transactions. As for the Manafea Saudi platform, it adopts a written risk 
management policy that encompasses multiple aspects such as credit, market, operational, and 
compliance risks, among others. It also has a credit rating system to assess risks associated with 
financing opportunities. This has contributed to reducing default rates, which totaled 1.232% by 
the end of 2024, increasing the use of crowdfunding by entrepreneurs and startups, enhancing the 
confidence of current and potential investors, and minimizing risks.

Abstract:

diversification in Algeria. The proposed applications offer practical solutions that leverage FinTech 
innovations while respecting religious values and cultural contexts, potentially serving as a 
blueprint for similar emerging markets. Furthermore, the study's findings aim to provide actionable 
insights for policymakers, businesses, and entrepreneurs seeking to capitalize on the opportunities 
presented by Islamic FinTech in the digital era.

Abstract :  
Banks perform the financial intermediation function between surplus units and deficit units. These banks 
emerged within the secular capitalist economic framework as market institutions aimed at maximizing 
profits, with loan returns and risk-trading activities being among their primary sources of income. 
Islamic societies needed financial intermediation institutions, but the conflict between conventional 
banking practices and Sharia principles necessitated the development of a new model of financial 
intermediation that fulfills the Sharia objectives regarding ownership and circulation of wealth. This model 
is based on realizing the social and economic functions of wealth in Islam. However, various factors 
hindered its practical implementation, leading to the adoption of a capital-based banking model compliant 
with Sharia transactional rules. In doing so, Sharia-compliant banks relied on juristic stratagems and 
financial engineering to structure contracts that emulate the functions of usurious and speculative contracts 
without outright contravening religious texts. 
Sharia-compliant banks have been able to offer the services provided by interest-based banks, albeit with 
lower efficiency due to Sharia constraints and restrictions. Therefore, the future of these banks is closely 
tied to the evolution of alternative interest-free intermediation institutions. 
The global shift toward achieving sustainable development has integrated economic and social 
development and led to the establishment of social financing and investment institutions that prioritize 
social objectives within economic investments. This trend has diminished the role of conventional banks 
and expanded the domain of solidarity-based social financial activities. 
The Expected Future of Islamic Banks: 
As Islamic countries adopt the Sustainable Development Goals, the relative importance of conventional 
banks will decline, making way for banking models that pursue the Sharia objectives of wealth generation 
and circulation. The Sharia objective of “reclaiming the earth” necessitates sustainable development 
centered on humanity and the purpose of creation. Consequently, Islamic banks must embrace the Sharia 
perspective in wealth creation and circulation to serve these objectives and support sustainable 
development.

 The paper presents an overview of Islamic finance and its connection to economic development. It outlines 
the vision of Islamic finance as a system aiming for societal betterment by adhering to Islamic laws 
(Shariah) and promoting justice across private, public, and voluntary sectors. The paper further explains 
the fundamental link between Islamic finance and economic development, highlighting its distinct 
principles such as the prohibition of interest and emphasis on real economic activity. While acknowledging 
positive contributions in areas like health and infrastructure, the text also points out limitations in its 
widespread adoption and impact on large-scale development. Finally, it proposes future directions for 
Islamic finance, advocating for a more holistic approach that moves beyond mere contractual compliance 
to focus on core principles and societal outcomes, incorporating new technologies and diverse financial 
models.

Abstract: 
This paper analyses the development and challenges of Islamic finance in Algeria over the past 50 years, focusing 
on legal milestones and obstacles and economic contributions. It aims to assess the factors influencing the 
development of Islamic financial instruments within the Algerian legal framework. Through qualitative research, 
including legal and data analysis, the study highlights the historical and market development of the three pillars 
of finance - banking, insurance and financial market, the impact of the introduction of Islamic finance and the 
identification of the main challenges, and emphasises the role of Islamic finance in the development of the Algerian 
economy. The findings suggest that the delay in launching Islamic finance in Algeria can be remedied through 
legal reforms, regulatory amendments, workforce education, and digitisation, Algeria can unlock the full potential

atteindre entre 8 381 et 25 667 milliards de dinars, reflétant l’impact des réformes et de l’innovation 
financière.

pilier essentiel du système bancaire algérien, contribuant à la diversification de l’offre financière et à une

to meet new challenges and could expand to 4618 branches by that time. The Islamic banking network, 
although more recent, is also expected to grow, with projections ranging between 924 and 3233 branches,

financial innovation. Thus, by fostering a favourable environment for expansion, Islamic finance could become 
a key pillar of the Algerian banking system, contributing to the diversification of financial services and greater 
financial inclusion.

 Abstract: 
The global financial crisis that struck the world economy in 2008 exposed the fragility of the liberal interest-
based banking and financial system. What began as a subprime mortgage crisis in the United States quickly evolved 
into a financial crisis affecting both financial and non-financial institutions, with its repercussions spreading to 
the real economy and transmitting contagion across all global economies, thereby undermining confidence in the 
nature of the international financial system. This opened the field for Islamic banking to assert its presence as the 
most prominent face of the Islamic economic system, poised to stand as an equal to Western economic models in 
a contest where victory belongs to those armed with policies and instruments capable of hedging against financial 
crises and ensuring they do not recur. Accordingly, this study aims to shed light on the extent to which Islamic 
banks were impacted by this crisis, to highlight their efficiency as a financing approach that avoids triggering 
financial crises, and to examine their role in mitigating the severity of such fluctuations. 
Keywords: financial crisis, Islamic banks, financial stability, performance of Islamic banks.

Abstract: 
This study aims to highlight the importance of Sharia auditing as a central and neutral tool in the Sharia 
compliance systems of Islamic financial institutions today. The paper also seeks to discuss the role of this 
type of auditing in the Islamic windows of conventional banks, as well as to review the mechanisms for 
activating it at various levels, including Sharia compliance, its effectiveness in the context of continuous 
improvement within the industry, and the development of a promising future path for these windows. 
Through the review and analysis of several studies and the experiences of some banks in this field, it became 
evident that there is an increasing interest in Sharia auditing in conventional banks due to the urgent need 
to provide transparency and legitimacy to financial products. The study showed that since the issuance of the 
Islamic banking system law (02-20) in Algeria, banks have seen a significant improvement in the application 
of organized Sharia auditing. Although the existence of Sharia compliance and auditing systems within these 
banks is commendable, with at least two bodies in the organizational structure (one for fatwa and another 
for Sharia auditing), along with a national fatwa body recognized by the central bank, the study revealed 
several challenges. These challenges include the lack of a clear legal framework for Islamic windows, 
insufficient support from the central bank, and a shortage of specialized personnel in the field of Sharia 
auditing. 
Keywords: Sharia auditing, Islamic windows, Sharia compliance.

The Reality and Challenges of Implementing Governance in Algerian Islamic Banks : A Case Study 
of Al Salam Bank 
 
 
 
Abstract: 
This study aimed to illustrate the reality of corporate governance implementation in Algerian Islamic banks 
and highlight the main challenges facing its application in the Algerian banking system, given the specific 
nature of the Algerian economy. For this purpose, the inductive approach and descriptive method were 
adopted. As for the case study conducted at Al Salam Bank - Algeria, which is one of the banks operating 
according to Islamic Sharia principles, the analytical method was adopted using a questionnaire tool. A total 
of 35 questionnaires were distributed, and the information 
collected was analyzed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS V21). The study 
concluded with several findings, the most important of which is that Algerian Islamic banks apply corporate 
governance principles, especially Al Salam Bank - Algeria, which operates according to the principles of 
transparency, information disclosure, Sharia compliance and auditing, corporate governance principles, and 
other related principles.

Abstract: 
Considering that financial statements are the backbone of decision-making in organizations and also the 
mirror of organization's activity, and since Islamic banks are distinguished from their conventional 
counterparts in many terms, perhaps their reliance on Islamic shariaa in all their transactions was the most 
prominent, it was necessary for this mirror to reflect this distinction. The study aimed to clarify the impact 
of the islamic accounting standards issued by the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial 
Institutions (AAOIFI) in expressing this specificity, by highlighting the most important differences between

Abstract:  
This study examines Islamic governance level in Islamic banks through the Islamic Reporting Initiative (IRI) 
Model, focusing on the Jordanian Islamic Bank (JIB) between 2019 and 2023. This research assesses the 
extent to which JIB aligns with the IRI Model’s key criteria, and how these contribute to enhanced Islamic 
governance and stakeholder trust. This study useda content analysis methodology based on the JIB’s reports 
between (2019-2023) and finds that the JIB has complete compliance with sharia governance, while showing 
a lack in some IRI disclosure criteria (Development of STEM Skills and Knowledge Transfer, Youth 
Engagement, Health Provision and Promotion). The study concludes with recommendations for strengthening 
disclosure mechanisms to ensure greater transparency and regulatory compliance in the bank. 
Keywords: Islamic banks, Islamic governance, Disclosure, Islamic Reporting Initiative (IRI), Jordanian Islamic 
Bank.

Absract : 
This paper, using the inductive method for description and analysis, aims to examine the adequacy of higher 
authorities established to ensure the compliance of Islamic financial industry institutions with Islamic law. It 
assesses their structure and function against the standards of independence and effectiveness established in 
international and comparative public business law to determine their nature and the authority of their 
opinions, particularly whether they qualify as regulatory oversight bodies. The study concludes that most of 
these authorities function as advisory bodies (fatwa-issuing entities) rather than regulatory ones, as legislators 
have merely authorized them to provide non-binding opinions. Even where certain legislations formally 
mandate compliance, this obligation remains superficial due to the lack of enforcement mechanisms, such as 
legally binding administrative decisions enforceable by law and subject to judicial review, as required by 
legislative principles. Consequently, it is necessary to amend the legal provisions governing these bodies to 
establish rigorous Sharia governance from the outset and, in the broader transition toward a participatory 
economy, to enact laws for economic and financial regulation. A unified legal framework is also essential to 
eliminate incidental dualities and contradictions in the system. 
Keywords: Sharia supervision, economic regulation, Sharia governance, Islamic finance, Islamic banking, 
Takaful insurance.

Abstract:

Institution in unifying the sharia reference for the islamic financial industry, In order to achieve this, the

Abstract : 
Sharia governance is one of the most critical components of Islamic banking, serving as the guiding compass 
for banks and their various units and departments. Saudi Arabia stands as one of the pioneering countries in 
this field, ranking among the global leaders in Islamic finance. 
Given this leadership, the Saudi experience presents valuable lessons, particularly in light of the governance 
framework issued by the Saudi Arabian Monetary Authority (SAMA). This study aims to shed light on that 
framework and explore how its principles can be adapted to the Algerian banking sector to develop a 
governance framework that aligns with Algeria’s economic and legal environment. 
The study is structured into three key sections. The first section discusses the theoretical framework of Sharia 
governance and its objectives. The second examines the history and contributions of Islamic banking in Saudi 
Arabia. Finally, the third section highlights the governance framework and identifies key elements that can 
be leveraged to develop an effective Sharia governance system in Algeria. Given the absence of a structured 
governance framework in Algeria, this deficiency may negatively impact the operations of Islamic banks, 
potentially undermining their credibility and transparency .

Abstract: 
This research aims to study and analyze the regulatory and legal environment for adopting Islamic banking 
and dealing with its financing and investment products, by highlighting the role of the Supreme Islamic 
Council from a legal perspective and the legal regulation of the Central Bank of Algeria.  
The research concluded that the National Sharia Authority for Fatwas for the Islamic Financial Industry has 
made significant efforts regarding the legal aspect of adopting Islamic banking, issuing a Sharia compliance 
certificate to banks wishing to deal with financial products that comply with the provisions of Islamic Sharia. 
This plays a regulatory and supervisory role over the operations of these institutions, in addition to issuing 
fatwas on issues necessary for the transition to Islamic banking. Furthermore, the Bank of Algeria defined 
banking operations related to Islamic banking and the rules for their practice by banks and financial 
institutions in Regulation No. 20-02 dated March 15, 2020. Despite these achievements, the Algerian banking 
environment still needs further work at the level of training and education of bank employees on the 
principles and foundations of Islamic financial transactions, not to mention holding conferences that bring 
together specialists. 
Keywords: Islamic banking, Shariah supervision, Islamic financial products, regulatory and Shariah 
frameworks, Supreme Islamic Council

Abstract:

numerous contemporary issues and complex emergent cases have arisen. These are unfamiliar to earlier 
scholars, leaving many people hesitant or uncertain about their permissibility or religious ruling. Among the 
most prominent areas in need of jurisprudential clarification today are financial transactions, due to the

500 Sharia Industry Exclusions ETF. 
Dr. Isma BELMIHOUB 
University of Bordj Bou Arreridj,Algeria 
isma.belmihoub@univ-bba.dz 
Abstract 
The Islamic finance industry has experienced huge expansion as interest in Shariah-compliant investing has 
increased globally; many innovative Islamic products imitate conventional finance instruments and some of 
them such as Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) are designed to truck Islamic indices being parts of larger 
conventional indices. This paper aims to analyze the role of conventional Indices as benchmarks for Islamic 
ETFs. 
Based on data published on trading platforms such as Statmuse, Trackinsight, Tindal and the ETF’s factsheets, 
this study employs an empirical approach to test the existence of a Granger causality among the conventional 
index “S&P 500” and the Islamic ETF “SP Sharia Industry Exclusions Fund” (SPUS). While focusing on the 
performance criterion over 5-year period monthly, a VECM is estimates the long-run relationship between 
the Index and the ETF.  
Thestudy concludes that conventional market indices have strong effects on Islamic ETFs returns. Besides, 
the empirical study finds a strong correlation among SP500 and SPUS. The Granger causality test concluded 
to a causal relationship from the SP500 towards the SPUS. Furthermore, the VECM estimation suggests that 
the relationship between the changes in the performance of the Islamic Fund (SPUS) is inversely related to 
its changes over a three-month period. While it is directly related to the changes in the performance of the 
“S&P 500 Index” over the three-month period.  
Keywords: Halal Exchange-Traded Funds,Sharia-compliant Indices, Conventional Indices benchmarks, 
Granger causality.

Abstract 
This research paper aims to estimate the technical and scale efficiency of Islamic banks operating in the Gulf 
Cooperation Council (GCC) countries and assess their performance. To achieve this objective, the Data 
Envelopment Analysis (DEA) approach will be employed within the framework of the production function, 
using a sample of 23 banks over the period 2010–2023. The analysis will be conducted from both input-
oriented and output-oriented perspectives, with results compared across different levels, including year, bank, 
and country. 
The findings indicate that several banks, namely Bank AlJazira, Bank Albilad, Kuwait Finance House, Warba 
Bank, Qatar Islamic Bank, Dukhan Bank, Al Salam Bank, and Alizz Islamic Bank, have attained the "Best 
Practice" level of efficiency, encompassing overall technical efficiency, pure technical efficiency, and scale 
efficiency. These banks have demonstrated optimal management of their internal and external operations, 
effectively utilizing their available resources compared to other banks. This efficiency has enabled them to 
achieve the optimal scale of activities and services relative to their available inputs. 
The study recommends examining the factors contributing to the decline in efficiency observed in some 
banks' internal and external operations. Additionally, it emphasizes the importance of raising awareness and 
enhancing education through workshops and training programs on modern quantitative methods in the 
banking sector. These methods play a crucial role in providing data that can help improve bank efficiency, 
address areas of weakness, and support policymakers in designing banking policies that align with economic 
efficiency requirements. 
Keywords: Scale Efficiency; Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA); Technical Efficiency

Abstract: 
As an Islamic financing instrument, the innovative sukuk as known today is a manifestation of a long journey 
of financial instruments suftaja/h,sakk, andesham in the history of Islamic civilization. To develop public 
financial instruments, indeed, it is important to trace their institutional history, especially those that have 
effectively overcome past challenges. In its time,suftaja/hwas a financial leap forward that existed for Muslim 
business people as a payment system to the public exchequer. Then, sakk was used for international trade and 
various commercial activities in Muslim territories during the Middle Ages. It served as a payment order to 
transfer financial obligations or ownership. Likewise, as the milestone for the presence of the world's first 
Islamic securitization, esham attested potent as a fiscal instrument to raise funds from the public. The Ottoman 
Empire developed eshamto face a crisis after the war's defeat. Therefore, to take lessonsfrom the institutional 
history of sukuk, this study aims to provide insight into the practices of suftaja/h,sakk, and esham as the 
forerunners of sukuk across history and compare them with the practices of sukuk and its Islamic blended 
finance in modern times through a historical literature review. 
Keywords:esham; sukuk; blended finance; green economy; green finance; Islamic blended finance; Islamic 
economics; Islamic finance; Islamic fiscal sustainability; Islamic sustainable finance; Ottoman Empire; 
sustainability.

Abstract 
This study aims to analyze the determinants of profitability in Islamic banks, based on a sample of eight Arab 
Islamic banks over the period (2011–2020). To achieve this objective, dynamic panel data models (Models 
Data Panel Dynamic) were adopted using the Generalized Method of Moments (GMM). 
The results revealed three statistically significant explanatory variables. The study found a statistically 
significant inverse relationship between both liquidity and the cost-to-income ratio with profitability, 
represented by the return on assets. Conversely, the results showed a significant positive relationship between 
capital adequacy and profitability. Meanwhile, no significant relationship was found between bank size and 
profitability. 
Keywords: Islamic banks, profitability, dynamic panel data, Generalized Method of Moments (GMM).

Open Banking business model as a new approach to providing financial services. This model allows customers 
to access their financial data through unified gateways and use it to access a wide range of new financial

Abstract: 
This study aims to review the Saudi experience in empowering nonprofit sector institutions to capitalize on 
the advantages and opportunities of artificial intelligence, and to propose an integrated framework for 
expanding the use of AI tools in the Saudi nonprofit sector to support Vision 2030, in light of current 
implementation realities and development challenges. 
The study found that Saudi nonprofit organizations have benefited from the services of the National Center 
for Nonprofit Sector Development and from the establishment of specialized AI institutions that have aided 
their digital transformation and empowerment. The research also revealed that many important AI tools—
such as big data analytics, smart endowment sukuk, neural networks, fuzzy logic, and machine learning—
have not yet been applied in the sector, despite their potential to drive a qualitative leap and a breakthrough 
in digital transformation and excellence. 
The study recommends developing crowdfunding platforms and innovating smart endowment sukuk based 
on blockchain technology as a new approach to improving the efficiency of endowment investment 
management and supporting financial empowerment in the Saudi nonprofit sector.

Résumé : 
La technologie financière est un moteur de succès dans le secteur financier, qui occupent une importance 
majeure dans l’économie du pays. Surtout après la mise en place d’une finance qui se conforme à la charia 
dans les banques.   
Le but de cette recherche est d’identifier la contribution de la technologie financière dans le développement 
de la finance islamique en Algérie. Pour ce faire, nous avons opté pour une recherche qualitative basée sur 
l’analyse documentaire, l’observation et des entretiens au niveau de la banque Extérieure d’Algérie. Les 
résultats de notre étude nous confirment que la mise en place de la technologie financière contribue à 
l’évolution de la finance islamique, mais la réglementation et le manque de développement en technologie 
dans les banques constitue un handicape pour l’évolution de la numérisation des transactions financières

Abstract : 
Financial technology is a driver of success in the financial sector, which is of major importance for the 
execution of financial transactions. Especially after the establishment of finance that complies with Sharia law 
in banks.  
The aim of this research is to identify the contribution of financial technology in the development of Islamic 
finance in Algeria. For this purpose, we opted for a qualitative research based on analysis of document, 
observation and interviews at the External Bank of Algeria. The results of our study allow us to confirm that 
the implementation of financial technology contributes to the improvement of in Islamic finance, but the 
regulation and the lack of development in technology in banks constitute a handicap for the evolution of the 
digitalization of Islamic financial transactions.  
Keywords : financial technology, Islamic finance, digitalization, Islamic financial transactions.

Abstract :  
This article aims to explore the potential of employing Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-
Augmented Generation (RAG) technology in developing intelligent chatbots for Islamic banks. The article 
discusses the fundamental concepts of Islamic Fintech and chatbots, then focuses on RAG technology as an 
innovative methodology to enhance the performance of chatbots in this sector. The article reviews the 
components of RAG technology and the necessary knowledge base for its application in the context of Islamic 
banks, emphasizing the importance of Sharia sources, institutional sources, and operational content. 
The study demonstrates that RAG technology offers effective solutions for developing more accurate, reliable, 
and Sharia-compliant chatbots in the Islamic Fintech sector. It also highlights the importance of this 
technology in continuously updating knowledge and customizing the knowledge base to meet the needs of 
Islamic banks. Despite the significant potential, the article points out that the theoretical framework for 
chatbot applications in Islamic Fintech remains limited, particularly concerning Sharia compliance, financial 
literacy, and integration with Islamic financial systems. 
The article recommends focusing on developing and expanding the theoretical framework for chatbot 
applications in Islamic Fintech, along with conducting further research and applied studies to evaluate the 
effectiveness of RAG technology in this field. It also calls for unifying Sharia standards and developing 
regulatory frameworks to support the growth and adoption of these technologies in the Islamic financial 
sector. 
Keywords: Chatbots, Large Language Models (LLMs), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Islamic 
Fintech, Islamic Banks, Sharia Compliance.

of Al Rajhi Bank in Saudi Arabia as a leading model. It does so by reviewing the theoretical concepts related

Abstract: 
This study aims to investigate the contribution of Islamic finance in attracting foreign direct investment (FDI) 
in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries during the period 2011-2022. The study analyzed the 
reality of Islamic finance in various regions of the world and presented the methodology for calculating the 
Islamic Finance Index. To determine the contribution of Islamic finance in increasing the proportion of FDI 
inflows, a panel model was used. After conducting the tests for this model, our analysis was based on the 
Fully Modified Least Squares (FMOLS) method. The study concluded that Islamic finance contributes to 
increasing FDI inflows in the long term. It also showed that the GCC countries rank first in total Islamic 
finance assets.

Abstract  
This study aims to highlight the reality of the use of electronic means of payment in light of the developments 
and rapid changes in the field of fintech and digital transformations witnessed in the banking and financial 
sector by examining the application of electronic means of payment at the Algiers Peace Bank as well as the 
challenges of its application.

Abstract: 
This study aims to explore the digital transformation within the Islamic financial industry from 2013 to 
2023, shedding light on the opportunities and challenges posed by this transformation in the context of the 
Fourth Industrial Revolution. It also evaluates its impact on the performance and operational strategies of 
Islamic banks. 
The study concludes that digital transformation has become a strategic necessity rather than a mere option, 
as it has led to improved operational efficiency, enhanced customer experiences, and increased financial 
returns. However, the level of adoption remains geographically uneven, with Southeast Asia and the Middle 
East leading the way, while other regions face regulatory and structural challenges. Furthermore, the study 
highlights the pivotal role of financial technology in advancing Islamic banking services, particularly through 
the use of artificial intelligence, blockchain, and cloud computing, which have contributed to promoting 
financial inclusion and developing innovative solutions such as digital sukuk and Islamic crowdfunding.

Bridging the Artificial Intelligence Technologies Gap in Islamic Banks : "Algeria's case study" 
 
 
 
Abstract: 
Artificial intelligence is one of the key industries of the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4.0). Our study provides 
practical solutions to bridge the gap in the application of artificial intelligence in Islamic banks by addressing 
issues related to Sharia compliance Infrastructure and Management. It also evaluates the maturity of artificial 
intelligence within organizations to offer effective solutions. This is achieved through a qualitative approach 
by conducting an interview with one of the managers of Bank of Al Salam in Algeria, which was analyzed 
Using qualitative data analysis software QDA miner lite. The study's results indicated that the bank manager 
is concerned about the sensitive data associated with banks and the ethical issues related to artificial 
intelligence. It also revealed that the overall maturity level of artificial intelligence within the organization is 
still in the "experimental" phase. 
Keywords: Islamic banks, AI, Islamic finance, shari’ah.

Emerging Trends in Blockchain Adoption and Its Impact on the Evolution of the Islamic Financial 
Industry: A Case Study of the United Arab Emirates . 
 
 
 
 
Abstract: 
In recent years, a groundbreaking technological innovation has emerged—Blockchain technology. Initially 
met with skepticism and outright rejection by major financial institutions, this technology has now garnered 
immense interest, with institutions willing to invest millions of dollars to master its optimal application. This 
paradigm shift is driven by the unparalleled advantages that blockchain offers, with expectations that it will 
profoundly transform business sectors. According to reports from esteemed sources such as Forbes, institutions 
that fail to adapt to this technological evolution may face obsolescence. 
The findings of this study indicate that modern financial technologies, including blockchain, have already 
made inroads into the Islamic financial industry, despite being in their nascent stages. This signals a 
forthcoming revolution in the sector, paving the way for transformative changes in the Islamic financial 
landscape. Accordingly, this research aims to shed light on the future of the Islamic financial industry in an 
era of increasing reliance on blockchain technology, with a particular focus on the United Arab Emirates—
one of the pioneering leaders in this field within the Arab and Islamic world. 
Keywords: Blockchain technology, Islamic financial industry, UAE experience.

Abstract :  
This study examines the role of Islamic financial instruments, particularly Green Sukuk, in supporting the achievement 
of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in Malaysia. Green Sukuk is a Sharia-compliant financing instrument 
designed to fund environmentally friendly projects, aligning with sustainability values in Islam. This research adopts 
an analytical approach through an in-depth literature review and library research to explore the potential and 
contribution of Green Sukuk in promoting sustainable development .The findings indicate that Green Sukuk can play 
a strategic role in financing projects that support environmental conservation in Malaysia, renewable energy, and the 
sustainable management of natural resources. Furthermore, the implementation of Green Sukuk demonstrates 
adherence to Sharia principles, which emphasize justice and ecological balance, thereby generating added value for both 
society and the environment ;However, challenges remain in the implementation of Green Sukuk, including regulatory 
issues, transparency, and reporting standards that require further harmonization.

Analysis of Some Case Studies. 
 
 
 
 
Abstract: 
This study investigates the contribution of Sustainable Sukuk in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals 
(SDGs), as set by the United Nations (UN). This research was conducted through literature studies and library 
research to explore the concept of Sustainable Sukuk, the SDGs, as well as the potential and the contribution 
of these Sukuk in achieving the SDGs. Furthermore, this study includes two case studies onthe application of 
Sustainable Sukuk in the form of Green Sukuk financing renewable energy and energy efficiency projects, as 
well as conductsan analysis of the socio-economic impacts of these projects and their contribution towards 
achieving the SDGs.The results of this study support the findingsof many previous studies, which concluded 
that sustainable sukuk contribute to achieving the SDGs. The first case studyshowed that the green sukuk 
issued by the Saudi Electricity Company align with SDG 7 and SDG 13, while the second case study stated 
that the sovereign green sukuk issued by the Indonesian Government align with SDG 8, SDG 10, and SDG11.

The Integration of Cash Waqf into the Management of Customary Land for the Empowerment of 
Indigenous People : An Analysis Based on Maqāṣid al-Sharī'ah.
 
 
 
 
Abstract : 
As a country with the largest customary territory in the world (30,108,515 Ha), Indonesia faces complex problems 
in providing legal certainty and maximizing benefits for indigenous peoples. With a majority Muslim population, 
Islamic philanthropy products can be a profitable option to increase the potential utilization of customary land 
(Tanah Ulayat). Cash waqf is considered more progressive in providing higher value benefits because Indonesia 
has been recognized as a regional leader in the issuance of cash waqf in ASEAN. Therefore, a study is needed 
regarding the law of integrating cash waqf in the management of Customary land for the empowerment of 
Indigenous peoples from the perspective of maqāṣid al-syarī’ah. This research uses qualitative research and 
normative legal research to develop arguments, theories, and practical solutions for identified legal issues. This 
research will use a conceptual approach in analyzing the law of integrating cash waqf with customary land for the 
empowerment of Indigenous peoples with the theory of maqāṣid al-syarī’ah by al-Syāṭibi, specifically in the 
application of the concept of Kulliyāt al-dīn al-khams. The data used is primary data from various regulations, 
fatwas, or official documents in the utilization and management of Cash waqf, which is supported by various 
secondary data from journals and other research. The results show that the concept of integrating cash waqf with 
customary land can be a good choice for both the Islamic Financial Institution Recipient of Cash Waqf (LKS-
PWU) and the indigenous people themselves to support the welfare of the community in general. With the right 
model, the integration of cash waqf on customary land can fulfill the principles of waqf management (sharia, 
usefulness, value growth, and sustainability). This model also has various advantages and challenges to be applied 
in indigenous communities. With various possible uses, the integration of cash waqf on customary land has fulfilled 
the Kulliyāt al-dīn al-khams formulated by al-Syāṭibi. This research is expected to provide recommendations and 
guidelines to stakeholders, cash waqf managers, Indigenous community leaders, and various other stakeholders in 
implementing the integration of cash waqf in the management of Customary land for the empowerment of 
Indigenous peoples. 
Keywords: Tanah Ulayat, Indigenous People, Kulliyāt al-dīn al-khams, al-Syāṭibi, Waqf Management.

The Impact of WaqfPreneur (Islamic Endowment Manager) Empowerment on Productive Cash 
Waqf : An Agent-Based Simulation.
 
 
 
 
Abstract : 
This study develops a direct partnership scheme for productive cash waqf and examines its economic 
outcomes using agent-based modeling. Employing an Agent-Based Model (ABM), the study creates an IISCF 
model that explores productive cash waqf through direct agent collaboration, considering variations in 
waqfpreneur number, coverage, and beneficiary share. The developed model demonstrates the positive long-
term empowerment of cash waqf by simulating the behavior of different agents. Specifically, increasing the 
beneficiary share percentage within the IISCF framework, alongside increases in waqfpreneur numbers and 
coverage, enhances the development of productive waqf assets and optimizes their empowerment to meet 
societal economic needs.Within the IISCF context, there is a lack of ABM research that incorporates 
productive cash waqf while accounting for the behavioral factors of society, waqf donors (waqif), and 
waqfpreneurs (nazhir or waqf managers with entrepreneurial skills). This simulation was limited to a specific 
number of scenarios and model assumptions tailored to the Indonesian context. Future research could 
broaden the experiment to explore the model's impact on wider socio-economic factors and utilize more 
extensive research assumptions, while adhering to Sharia principles. Academics, practitioners, policymakers, 
and waqf regulators can adopt this model to assess behavioral interactions among the three agent types within 
the system. 
Keywords:Agent-Based Model, productive cash waqf, IISCF, direct partnership, waqfpreneur.

Abstract: 
This study aims to highlight the pivotal role that green Islamic sukuk play in supporting and financing green 
projects and investments in Malaysia, which directly contribute to the achievement of sustainable 
development goals in the country.

conceptual framework on green Islamic sukuk. The analytical approach was used in the practical aspect to 
analyze the reality of financing green investments through sukuk in Malaysia and evaluate their impact on

Abstract:

of water endowment in supporting diverse activities for both individuals and society as a whole, thereby ensuring the 
achievement of sustainable development goals—particularly the sixth goal, which pertains to the provision of safe 
drinking water and sanitation services. Subsequently, the paper explores the role of the Kuwaiti Direct Aid Association

Abstract:  
The growing focus on sustainability globally represents an opportunity for growth and collaboration in the field of 
sustainable Islamic finance. Similarly, green finance can be viewed as a comprehensive paradigm shift towards future 
financing decisions, extending to the sustainability of the entire ecosystem by promoting green growth. The Islamic 
finance industry has shown remarkable growth in recent years, reaching a global value of over US$4 trillion and 
maintaining steady expansion year on year. However, despite the inherent alignment between Islamic principles and 
ethical and socially conscious values, the global Islamic finance sector has yet to fully embrace the broader world of 
sustainable finance. However, there is a significant and concerted effort within the Islamic finance industry to change 
this trajectory. The increasing focus on sustainability globally represents an opportunity for growth and collaboration 
in the Islamic finance space, as frameworks such as the Principles for Responsible Banking can provide an accelerated 
path for Islamic financial institutions to achieve sustainable development goals, continue their journey towards positive 
impacts on society and the environment, while continuing to enhance stakeholder value.

Abstract: 
This research paper aims to identify the main challenges facing green Islamic sukuk in financing sustainable projects. 
Green Islamic sukuk seek to align sustainability requirements with Islamic values based on justice, transparency, and 
social responsibility. Despite the significant potential these sukuk offer in supporting the transition towards a green 
economy, their practical implementation faces a range of challenges. These include the absence of unified standards for 
classifying sukuk as "green," difficulties in accurately and transparently measuring environmental returns, limited 
investor awareness of such instruments, and the intersection of Shariah and environmental considerations in 
determining eligible projects for financing.

Abstract: 
This paper aims to highlight the complementarity between Islamic finance and the green economy, as the 
latter, which focuses on sustainable and environmentally sound growth, meets the principles of Islamic finance 
that prohibit usury and promote social justice. We also discuss how this complementarity can support the 
financing of sustainable projects, through the integration of green sukuk within the framework of Islamic

Abstract: 
Social enterprises are an important means of helping the government solve social problems, as 
the ultimate mission of the social enterprise is to address the most pressing social or environmental issues in 
society. Despite their importance, social enterprises in many countries face many challenges, the most 
important of which is the issue of financing. In Malaysia, the search for sustainable alternatives to finance 
social enterprises is a major concern for the government, stakeholders and researchers alike. As Malaysia is 
an Islamic country where zakat is an important source of finance that contributes to solving social problems, 
zakat institutions can provide appropriate financing for social enterprises. The aim of this study is to analyze 
previous studies and reports provided by specialized organizations on zakat institutions and their role in 
financing projects in general in order to gain a deeper understanding of the extent to which zakat institutions 
are willing to finance social enterprises and propose them as an alternative for social entrepreneurs. This 
study concluded that zakat institutions in Malaysia are willing to finance social enterprises through providing 
donations, granting good loans and entering into partnerships with social entrepreneurs.

Abstract: 
This paper aims to highlight the role of Islamic banks in fostering citizenship values and consolidating 
business ethics through their commitment to social responsibility, in accordance with the principles of Shariah 
law and Islamic economics. The study focuses on the experience of the Jordan Islamic Bank during the period 
2016-2023, presenting it as a practical model that reflects the extent of the commitment of Islamic banking 
institutions in achieving sustainable development. The research examines the regulatory framework and 
strategic approaches adopted by Islamic banks to fulfill their social responsibilities, analyzing the impact of 
these practices on economic development, social justice, and their contribution to strengthening citizenship 
values and business ethics. 
The findings confirm that the Jordan Islamic Bank’s contributions were not just limited to compliance with 
regulatory requirements but rather constituted an essential component of its institutional strategy. An analysis 
of the bank’s social responsibility reports highlights its tangible contributions to key sectors such as education, 
healthcare, and interest-free financing (Qard Hasan), reflecting its strong commitment to a sustainable 
developmental social role. The study concludes that the model adopted by the Jordan Islamic Bank establishes 
it as a pioneering example in Islamic banking, enhancing its capacity to effectivelycontribute to achieving 
economic and social objectives within a comprehensive developmental framework

‏إسلامية، وتوجيه الإنفاق العام لصيغ التمويل المتوافقة مع الشريعة. ‏
23
‏. تعزيز التكامل المالي الإسلامي بين الدول الإسلامية ‏
‏ ،من خلال فتح الأسواق، والاعتراف المتبادل بالرخص‏
‏وتوحيد النظم الضريبية والتنظيمية. ‏
24
‏. اقتراح إنشاء "مجلس عالمي لتنسيق سياسات المالية الإسلامية" ‏
‏ ،يجمع بين المنظمات الدولية، البنوك المركزية‏
‏ومؤسسات الرقابة، بهدف صناعة رؤية عالمية مشتركة. ‏
 
 

 
185 
 
 
Preamble 
On the occasion of the fiftieth anniversary of the inception of institutional Islamic finance, and 
in light of its subsequent global expansion, and in response to the profound transformations 
taking place in the international financial landscape — from digital transformation and evolving 
consumer behavior to regulatory challenges and geopolitical risks — this international 
conference was convened to assess the trajectory of Islamic finance, analyze its current 
outcomes, and develop strategic visions for its future. 
Following intensive scholarly deliberations involving a distinguished group of researchers, 
scholars, and practitioners from more than 25 countries, the conference concluded with the 
following recommendations: 
First: On Assessing the Fifty-Year Journey of the Islamic Financial Industry 
1. Call for comprehensive and periodic global assessment reports documenting the 
industry's development across all its components (banking, takaful, sukuk, investment, 
microfinance, and digital financial services), evaluating its real impact on development 
and economic justice, rather than merely quantitative growth indicators. 
2. Acknowledgment of the gap between theory and practice in Islamic financial 
institutions, and the need to narrow this gap by strengthening the bridges between 
Shariah scholars, practitioners, regulatory bodies, and economic researchers. 
3. Reorienting the industry's compass towards the higher objectives of Shariah, 
especially in promoting distributive justice, financing productive sectors, and 
minimizing negative impacts resulting from "Shariah arbitrage" in certain financial 
products. 
 
 

 
186 
 
 
Second: On Developing the Institutional and Regulatory Environment 
4. Modernizing national and international legal frameworks to accommodate the 
specificities of Islamic finance by adopting dual financial laws that allow Islamic 
institutions to operate within a legal environment consistent with their references. 
5. Enhancing the independence of Shariah supervisory boards within financial 
institutions, subjecting them to disclosure and governance standards comparable to 
those imposed on boards of directors, while reviewing and activating the roles of 
internal and external Shariah auditing. 
6. Standardizing Shariah, accounting, and regulatory practices across Islamic 
countries by strengthening the role of international institutions such as AAOIFI, IFSB, 
and the Islamic Financial Services Board, to reduce discrepancies that hinder 
integration. 
Third: On Islamic Banks and Their Products 
7. Restructuring the business models of Islamic banks to depart from near-complete 
replication of conventional banks, and increasing reliance on participatory financing 
modes (such as mudarabah, musharakah, istisna') rather than debt-based modes (such 
as murabaha and ijarah). 
8. Encouraging the development of Islamic financial products targeting small and 
medium enterprises and innovation sectors, alongside interest-free crowdfunding tools 
and direct financing platforms. 
9. Reviewing credit policies and risk management methods in Islamic banks to align 
with the nature of Islamic contracts, and activating preventive tools against default 
while maintaining the principle of risk-sharing. 
 
 

 
187 
 
Fourth: On the Takaful and Islamic Insurance Industry 
10. Transitioning from the hybrid commercial takaful model to a pure cooperative 
takaful model, and enhancing financial segregation between policyholders’ accounts 
and the operator’s account. 
11. Innovating Shariah-compliant insurance products that address contemporary risks 
(such as cybersecurity, climate change, and natural disasters), while developing fair 
pricing models consistent with the spirit of mutual cooperation. 
12. Promoting health and retirement takaful as a foundation for strengthening social 
justice in societies with fragile protection systems. 
Fifth: On Sukuk and Islamic Investment 
13. Expanding the use of sukuk as a developmental financing tool for infrastructure, 
renewable energy, and education, with the development of Shariah-based classification 
tools based on the activity and purpose of each sukuk. 
14. Launching waqf and development investment funds managed under principles of 
transparency and accountability, to invest in projects with sustainable economic and 
social impact. 
15. Enhancing the governance of international Islamic investments and integrating 
ethical, social, and environmental analysis tools in financing decisions. 
Sixth: On Islamic Digital Finance (FinTech) 
16. Building comprehensive digital Islamic financial platforms capable of delivering 
fully automated banking and financing services, leveraging artificial intelligence and 
blockchain technologies. 
17. Developing smart digital Shariah contracts to facilitate Islamic financial 
transactions without human intervention, with self-verifying compliance mechanisms. 

 
188 
 
18. Establishing national and regional Shariah sandboxes to test and develop 
innovative financial products and services in a flexible regulatory environment framed 
by Shariah guidelines. 
Seventh: On Education, Research, and Capacity Building 
19. Redesigning academic programs in Islamic finance to be interactive, 
interdisciplinary, and integrating Shariah sciences, digital economy, artificial 
intelligence, and strategic foresight. 
20. Supporting think tanks and specialized observatories dedicated to monitoring 
industry developments, analyzing challenges, and providing policy proposals to 
institutions and decision-makers. 
21. Launching advanced training programs and professional certifications in 
emerging fields such as digital Shariah auditing, Islamic risk management, and Shariah 
evaluation of innovative products. 
Eighth: On Public Policy and International Integration 
22. Encouraging governments to adopt Islamic financing policies within their 
development strategies, by establishing Islamic development banks and institutions 
and directing public spending toward Shariah-compliant financing formats. 
23. Promoting Islamic financial integration among Islamic countries by opening 
markets, mutual recognition of licenses, and harmonizing tax and regulatory systems. 
24. Proposing the creation of a Global Council for Islamic Finance Policy 
Coordination, bringing together international organizations, central banks, and 
supervisory institutions to develop a shared global vision.

Dr. Bouabdallah Ghoulamallah
Former President of High Islamic Council
Algeria
Dr. Bouabdallah Ghoulamallah served as President of the High 
Islamic Council of 
Algeria from 2012 to 2022 and was previously Minister of Religious 
Affairs. With a long 
academic and public service career, he is noted for modernizing 
religious education and promoting moderate Islamic values. He has 
been a strong advocate for social cohesion and religious reform.
Prof Dato’ Dr. Mohd Azmi Omar
President & Chief Executive Officer
INCEIF University, Malaysia.  
Prof. Dato’ Dr. Mohd Azmi Omar is the President and CEO of 
INCEIF University in Malaysia. He is a leading figure in Islamic 
finance with over 36 years of academic and institutional 
experience. He was a founding faculty member of the 
International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM), where he also 
served as Dean and Deputy Rector. Additionally, he led major 
initiatives as Director General of the Islamic Research and 
Training Institute (IRTI) at the Islamic Development Bank (IsDB).
53

Mr. Nasser Hideur
CEO of Al Salam Bank
Algeria
Mr. Nasser Hideur is the CEO of Banque Al Salam Algeria, the 
second-largest Islamic banking 
institution in the country. His professional career spans over 30 
years in Islamic banking, beginning at Banque Al Baraka Algeria, a 
renowned training ground for talent in this sector. He later moved 
to Banque Al Salam Algeria, where he held several key positions, 
starting as a legal and Shariah 
compliance officer, progressing to legal affairs manager, then 
secretary-general, before being appointed CEO in 2016.
Mr. Abdelmouneim Othmani Marabout
CEO of Al Baraka Bank 
Algeria
Mr. Abdelmouneim Othmani Marabout is a prominent figure in the 
Islamic banking sector in Algeria. He currently serves as the CEO of 
Al Baraka Bank Algeria, a leading Islamic financial institution with a 
strong presence in the Algerian market. He was appointed to this 
position in January 2025, bringing with him over three decades of 
experience in banking and finance.
54

Dr. Mabrouk Zaid El-Khair is the current President of the High 
Islamic Council of Algeria. A respected scholar with a PhD in 
linguistics and Quranic studies, he has held leadership roles in 
academia and national religious institutions. He is known for his 
work in promoting moderate Islamic thought, religious tolerance, 
and scholarly excellence.
Dr. Sami Al Suwailem is the Acting Director General of the Islamic 
Development Bank Institute (IsDBI) and Chief Economist at the 
Islamic Development Bank Group in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. He 
previously led R&D at Al-Rajhi Bank and held academic positions in 
the U.S. and Saudi Arabia. Dr. Al Suwailem has served on numerous 
professional committees related to Islamic finance and economics. 
He earned his M.A. from Southern Illinois University (1990) and 
Ph.D. from Washington University in St. Louis (1995). He is a 
published author in the field of Islamic economics and finance.

The Evolution of Islamic Financial Industry from the Ottoman 
Cash Waqfs to Modern Islamic Banks
Prof Dr. Mehmet Bulut
Sabahattin Zaim University
 Istanbul, Turkey
Abstract:
It is evident that in spite of some similarities the nature of characteristics of the political and 
economic aims of theempires and national states are different. It seems that in spite of some 
similarities in the aims, political economies and the institutions there are also some very critical 
differences between the Ottoman world and Western capitalist nations.While the Western 
European nations followed the protectionist mercantilist policies the Ottomans followed an open 
door economic policies towards the Atlantic nations in the early modern times.When we look at 
the institutions we have seen the waqfs, cash waqfs, ahidnames (capitulations), brotherhood (ahilik), 
iltizam, malikane and esham systems, etc. in the Ottoman world while the joint stock companies, 
modern banks based on interest, insurance companies and exchange stock market appeared in 
North Atlantic World in in the early modern times. These institutions played different roles in 
between the two worlds and civilisations. Especially the Ottoman cash waqfs are very critical as the 
first modern islamic bank institutions
